  "concordance_definition": "The paper does not explicitly define concordance between animal models and human clinical outcomes. It presents analyses of both murine models and human samples using the same pipeline and notes that \"HeartJ analysis revealed that human and murine cardiomyocytes are approximately equal in diameter and hypertrophy within a similar range.\"",
  "limitations_stated": [
    "The pipeline can only analyze parts of a WSI or individual images taken with a microscope.",
    "The current pipeline does not include fibrosis evaluation.",
    "Regions with marked destruction of cardiac histology such as infarct scars are not suitable for this type of histological analysis.",
    "The HeartJ immunofluorescence pipeline is not well applicable to human autopsy tissue due to high autofluorescence.",
    "The method is not based on deep learning technology, which could potentially improve automation and precision."
  ],
  "funding_conflict": null,
  "key_numbers": [
    "TAC was performed in five weeks old C57BL/6N mice",
    "Seven cases with Aortic (valve) stenosis and 14 cases with no clinical or autopsy findings of cardiac disease were selected for the human cohort",
    "Approximately, 750 cardiomyocytes were analyzed per animal in the murine study",
    "A total of 13% of false cardiomyocytes were excluded from the analysis in the murine study",
    "Approximately 4000 cardiomyocytes were analyzed per case in the human study",
    "The whole HeartJ pipeline procedure took less than one minute to analyze an image without manual corrections",
    "The time required for a manual correction of one image depended on the image quality and was between 2 and 6 min",
    "In sham animals, one cardiomyocyte had contact with three capillaries whereas in TAC animals this number was higher (3.1 ± 0.2 vs 3.6 ± 0.4; p = 0.0020)",
    "Almost no pro-ANP expression per cardiomyocyte in the sham animals and a significant, 33-fold increase of mean single cardiomyocyte expression of pro-ANP in TAC animals (0.06% ± 0.06% vs. 2.0% ± 2.0%; p = 0.0101)"
  ]
